title: Device and cable: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, the factors and overload

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the fuse's I2 pass the cable's 1.45 Iz in red, then meet it at 20.00 A as the cable's Iz rises to 13.79 A, when you choose the fuse and then apply Cf.
interactive.title: The device, the cable, the overload
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in twelve screens, with Back and Continue between them, on choosing the protective device and the cable it protects. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: “A heater circuit has In 16 A. The whole run is in a warm room, Ca 0.94. The cable is clipped direct, then runs in trunking with another circuit, Cg 0.8. Then it leaves the trunking and passes through a cavity wall with 50 mm of thermal insulation, Ci 0.88. What tabulated current It must the cable have?” Three choices, in this order: 19.34 A, 21.28 A, 24.18 A. Right: “Still there.” and the working, 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.8) = 21.28 A, the worse of the two places.[^1] A note says you may see it printed as 21.2 A, cut short. A line each on the slips: 24.18 A multiplies factors that never act together, and 19.34 A is the easier place. Two buttons: Refresh the why (on to screen 2) and Skip to the practice (straight to screen 7). Wrong, 24.18 A: apply rating factors together only when they happen together.[^2] The trunking and the insulation are in different places, so work each place on its own. Wrong, 19.34 A: that is the insulated part, 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.88).[^3] The trunking runs hotter and needs 21.28 A. The cable must survive its worst place. Then the right working and on to screen 2, with no skip. Read: It is 21.28 A, the worse of the two places. All three multiplied gives 24.18 A. Screen 2, What it is for: the chain Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, Regulation 433.1.1.[^4] The device's rating or current setting is at least the design current.[^5] The cable's current-carrying capacity where it is installed is at least the device's. The table's figure, It, is for a single circuit at the table's ambient.[^6] Iz is what the cable carries continuously where it actually runs.[^7] One more condition: I2, the current that finally operates the device, is no more than 1.45 Iz.[^8] In red, if it is skipped or wrong: a cable that makes heat faster than it can shed runs hot. Over time that damages insulation, joints, terminations and their surroundings.[^9] Screen 3, The why: the run in sections. Opening text: anything that makes the cable artificially warm needs a rating factor.[^10] Ca is for the ambient, Cg for grouping[^11] and Ci for insulation. Each one means the cable reaches its limit at a lower current. So the factors divide In to give the It the table must show.[^12] The picture: the heater circuit drawn as its route in three sections, left to right, named short on the drawing: Clipped (clipped direct), Trunking (in trunking with another circuit), Insulated wall (through the wall's insulation). Each section shows the factors acting there and the It it needs, worked from the figures shown: clipped, Ca 0.94: 16 ÷ 0.94 = 17.02 A; trunking, 0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752: 16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A; wall, 0.94 × 0.88 = 0.8272: 16 ÷ 0.8272 = 19.34 A. The section needing the highest It is outlined in ink and named. It sets the cable, and its reference method sets the column.[^13] This run has only two methods, B in the trunking and C clipped direct, and the design is to B. The wall has no column of its own here. Under the picture: the trunking needs the most, so it sets the cable. There the warm room starts the cable warmer, and the other circuit stops it shedding its heat. “Tap a section to read its working.” A switch, Insulation inside the trunking too: on, the trunking section has all three, 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.8 × 0.88) = 24.18 A. That is the one place where multiplying all three is right, and the outline stays on it. Two lines under it: Cg always counts the circuit being installed. A cable expected to carry not more than 30% of its grouped rating may be ignored when finding the factor for the rest of the group, Table 4C1 note 9.[^14] Read: the trunking sets the cable at 21.28 A. You get 24.18 A only if all three factors act in one place. Screen 4, The why: overload, two marks on one current line. Opening text: I2 is the current that makes the device operate. Most devices have an I2 of 1.45 times In.[^15] How long they take to operate at that current varies. One maker's type B breakers, from 6 to 63 A,[^59] operate within 1 hour. Its C breakers do the same.[^16] So do its D breakers.[^17] That hour is called the conventional time. Other figures run to 10,000 s, about 2.8 hours.[^60] The design does not hang on the time. The cable must carry I2 for as long as the device takes, so I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.[^18] That factor keeps small overloads from deteriorating the cable.[^19] The picture: one horizontal current axis from 0 to 25 A, the device's marks above it (In, and I2 in ink), the cable's below it (Iz, and 1.45 Iz). A named choice, Device: 10 A type B breaker, 10 A rewireable fuse. A switch, Apply Cf = 0.725, live only for the fuse. Breaker: I2 = 10 × 1.45 = 14.50 A.[^20] The cable is a 1.0 mm² twin and earth, Iz 13 A,[^21] and 1.45 × 13 = 18.85 A. I2 sits below it: “Passes”. Fuse: a BS 3036 fuse's I2 can be up to twice its rating, with the rating matched to the cable.[^22] 2 × 10 = 20.00 A is past 18.85 A, so the I2 mark turns red: “Fails: the cable could carry 20.00 A until the fuse opens”. Cf on: In must not exceed 0.725 Iz,[^23] so the cable needs Iz ≥ 10 ÷ 0.725 = 13.79 A.[^24] Then 1.45 × 13.79 = 20.00 A. The cable's marks rise and 1.45 Iz meets the fuse's I2: “Passes with Iz 13.79 A: the 13 A cable is too small behind this fuse”. Two lines: 0.725 is 1.45 ÷ 2, the breaker's 1.45 over the fuse's 2. Breakers to BS EN 60898 and fuses to BS 88 meet I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz whenever Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds, Regulation 433.1.201.[^51] The breaker here does. A rewireable fuse needs Cf, and a motor's thermal relay is checked on its maker's curve.[^52] The status line and the I2 and Iz figures change when the marks arrive. Read: a 10 A breaker's 14.50 A is within the 13 A cable's 18.85 A. A 10 A rewireable fuse reaches 20.00 A and needs a cable with Iz of 13.79 A. Screen 5, Check: “Seven circuits are bunched in one trunking. Four will each carry not more than 30% of their grouped rating. For the Cg of the other three, what is the fewest circuits you may count?” Choices: 7 (counting all seven is allowed and cautious, but note 9 lets the light ones go), 3 (right), 2 (the circuit being installed always counts). Why?: Table 4C1 note 9 lets you ignore the four.[^14] Each of the other three counts itself and the other two. Table 4C1 item 1 gives three circuits bunched 0.70.[^25] Read: three circuits count, Cg 0.70. Screen 6, Worked example, the heater circuit a line at each press: 0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752; 16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A;[^1] 0.94 × 0.88 = 0.8272; 16 ÷ 0.8272 = 19.34 A;[^3] design to 21.28 A, on Reference Method B, the method that cuts Iz most;[^13] 2.5 mm² from column 7 of Table 4D5. Then the overload check: I2 = 10 × 1.45 = 14.50 A;[^20] Iz 13 A;[^21] 13 × 1.45 = 18.85 A, above 14.50 A: the cable lasts.[^18] A last line: You may see 21.28 A printed as 21.2 A, cut short. Rounded, it is 21.3 A. 19.3 A and 14.5 A are rounded correctly. The cable size does not change. Screen 7, Section A, question 1 (c). The scenario panel gives the supply.[^26] It gives the room's ambient.[^27] It gives the motor.[^28] Parts (a) and (b) are carried forward. Given: the standard ratings near Ib are 16, 20, 25 and 32 A.[^29] “(c) Determine the smallest standard rating of the circuit-breaker at DBP2 for the motor circuit.” A typed answer, part 1c, in whole amperes: 25 A, the smallest not below Ib, 23.08 A.[^5] Slips: 16 A (below Ib: the breaker carries the line current, not the 15.88 A from the output alone or a winding's 13.33 A), 20 A (below Ib), 32 A (it would do, but 25 A is the smallest). After it comes the type, as a choice. A motor takes much more current starting than running.[^30] Its start-up current is high.[^31] A star-delta start draws roughly 2 to 2.7 times full-load current.[^32] Direct-on-line draws 6 to 8 times.[^33] These are rough guide figures, not a standard. Take 2.7 here, a practice value: 2.7 × 23.08 = 62.32 A. Use the motor maker's figure on a real job. Instantaneous trip at 25 A: type B 3 to 5 In, 75 to 125 A;[^34] type C 5 to 10 In, 125 to 250 A, the type for small motors;[^35] type D 10 to 20 In, 250 to 500 A.[^36] “Which type of breaker suits the practice start of 62.32 A?” Type B, Type C, Type D, each with its trip at 25 A. Right, C: it suits small motors. We take it here because it clears the start with more room than B. B: it clears 62.32 A too, but its trip starts at 75 A, with little room, and the real start may be higher. D: it clears the start by far more than it needs. Type D is for transformers, X-ray machines and industrial welding. One more go after a miss. Then the overload. We assume the starter's thermal relay sits in the delta circuit. There it is set to 0.58 × the motor's full-load current, from the nameplate.[^37] 0.58 is 1 ÷ √3, rounded. It is never set higher than the phase current,[^38] 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. That setting is the In of the starter-to-motor cables.[^5] After two misses the working shows, and part (d) carries on from 25 A. Read: 25 A, type C, our choice. The relay at 13.33 A guards the motor's cables against overload. Screen 8, Section A, question 1 (d): (a) to (c) carried forward. Given: the room is at 20 °C.[^27] Six 90 °C thermosetting singles run from the starter to the motor,[^39] sized on the delta running conditions.[^40] They share one conduit on the consultation bay's wall. We assume it is clear of insulation, so Ci and Cf are 1. First a choice, “How many circuits do the six singles count as for Cg?”: 6 (note 5 counts singles in threes), 3 (n/2 is for circuits of two loaded conductors, and these are three-phase), 2 (right). Its feedback: in delta running, all six carry winding current.[^41] For three-phase circuits, n singles count as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors.[^42] So the six make two circuits.[^43] Bunched and enclosed, two circuits take Cg 0.80, Table 4C1 item 1.[^25] Then Ca, labelled a practice value. Take Ca as 1.00 here. It takes no credit for the cool 20 °C room. Table 4B1 covers ambients other than 30 °C.[^44] Its first row, 25 °C, gives 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting.[^45] On a real job, check Table 4B1 for how to treat 20 °C. “(d) Taking Ca as 1.00, determine the minimum tabulated current-carrying capacity, It, of the starter-to-motor cables.” A typed answer, part 1d: 13.33 ÷ (1.00 × 0.80) = 16.66 A. Also accepted: 16.65 A, from the unrounded winding current, and 16.68 or 16.69 A, with √3 taken as 1.73. Slips: 13.33 A (Cg left out), 23.08 A (the line current, and Cg left out), 28.85 A (the line current: these cables carry a winding's), 31.25 A (the breaker's 25 A: the relay is their overload device), 16.34 A (Ca 1.02, the 25 °C row: fair in a design, but the question takes 1.00, and the cable comes out the same). Read: It ≥ 13.33 ÷ (1.00 × 0.80) = 16.66 A. Screen 9, Section A, question 1 (e) and (f): (a) to (d) carried forward. “(e) State the table and the column.” A choice: Table 4E1A, column 5, Method B, 3 or 4 cables (right); Table 4E1A, column 4, Method B, 2 cables, for single-phase; Table 4E1A, column 3, Method A, conduit in a thermally insulating wall. Feedback: non-armoured 90 °C thermosetting singles are in Table 4E1A.[^46] It has a column for Reference Method B.[^47] Conduit on a wall is Method B.[^48] Two three-phase circuits read the 3 or 4 cables column. “(f) Determine the minimum CSA of the starter-to-motor cables.” Under it: read column 5 in your copy of the table. A typed answer, part 1f, in mm²: 1.5. Slips: 1 (Cg left out: 13.33 A fits it), 2.5 (sized on the line current, 23.08 A), 4 (the line current ÷ 0.80, 28.85 A). Feedback: 1 mm² carries 15 A, under 16.66 A.[^49] 1.5 mm² carries 20 A, the smallest that passes.[^50] Then a note on the terminals. These are 90 °C ratings. They hold only if the starter's and motor's terminals are designed for 90 °C. If they are designed for less, rate the cables at the terminals' temperature, Table 4E1A note 1.[^61] At 70 °C, use Table 4D1A.[^62] Its column 5 gives 1.5 mm² only 15.5 A, under 16.66 A.[^63] So check the terminals before settling on 1.5 mm². Iz = 20 × 1.00 × 0.80 = 16.00 A, so 13.33 ≤ 13.33 ≤ 16.00. Iz 16.00 A is below the 25 A breaker at DBP2. So for these cables, that breaker gives protection against fault current only. Lesson 7 checks that. Regulation 433.1.201 does not list thermal relays, as screen 4 showed.[^51] So read the relay's curve from its maker.[^52] It must operate by 1.45 × 16.00 = 23.20 A. A conduit fixed to a masonry wall may carry more.[^53] We take no credit for that here. Read: Table 4E1A, column 5; 1.5 mm², Iz 16.00 A. Screen 10, Section B: “State a hazard of an overload current in a circuit, and explain how the design keeps a small overload from harming the cable.” His written answer is marked against four points. A full answer makes any three, so at least one hazard and one design point. One more go, then the model answer. Screen 11, Section A, changed numbers: “An older circuit is protected by a 15 A semi-enclosed (rewireable) fuse to BS 3036, and no other rating factor applies. Determine the minimum tabulated current-carrying capacity, It, of its cable.” A typed answer: 15 ÷ 0.725 = 20.69 A.[^24] Slips: 15.00 A (Cf left out), 10.88 A (multiplied by 0.725), 21.75 A (1.45 × 15: a breaker's I2, not It). Read: It ≥ 15 ÷ 0.725 = 20.69 A. Screen 12, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The line under the lesson reads: practice values are marked, and each line is worked from the rounded figures before it. It shows on screens 3, 4, 6 to 9 and 11.
interactive.ignores: The sections are drawn by the factors acting in them, not by a measured temperature. Each mark on the current line is a single figure. A real device operates within a band, and sooner the further the current is above In. The fuse's I2 is drawn at twice In, the figure Cf allows for. A particular fuse's I2 may be lower. Ca, Cg and Ci are treated as separate causes of heat, as the tables treat them. The 90 °C ratings assume the starter's and motor's terminals can run that hot. If they are designed for less, Table 4E1A note 1 rates the cables at the lower temperature. Short circuits and earth faults are other lessons. A device that protects against overload must still be checked for those.

explain.text:
The device protects the cable. So you choose the device from the load, and the cable from the device: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.[^4] The device's rating or setting must be at least the design current.[^5] The cable must carry at least that much where it runs hottest. A device also lets more than its rating flow for a while before it opens. The cable must survive that too: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.[^8]

Start with heat. The table's figure, It, is for one circuit at the table's ambient.[^6] What the cable can carry where it is actually installed is its [[current-carrying capacity]], Iz.[^7] Anything that makes the cable artificially warm needs a [[rating factor]].[^10] That means a hotter room, thermal insulation, or other circuits beside it. Ca is for the ambient, Cg for grouping[^11] and Ci for insulation. A warm room starts the conductor warmer. Neighbours or insulation stop it shedding its heat. Either way, a smaller current takes it to its maximum temperature, so the cable can carry less there. To carry In in that place, it needs a bigger table figure. That is why the factors divide: It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × Ci × Cf).[^12] A factor only counts where its heat is. You apply factors together only when they happen together.[^2] Take a heater circuit with In 16 A. The warm room, Ca 0.94, acts along the whole run. Grouping, Cg 0.8, acts only in the trunking. Insulation, Ci 0.88, acts only in the wall. So It is 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.8) = 21.28 A in the trunking.[^1] It is 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.88) = 19.34 A in the wall.[^3] You design the cable to the higher figure, on the reference method that cuts Iz the most.[^13]

Then the overload. I2 is the current that makes the device operate. Most devices have an I2 of 1.45 times In.[^15] So a 10 A breaker has an I2 of 14.50 A.[^20] Take a 1.0 mm² cable with an Iz of 13 A.[^21] It can take up to 1.45 × 13 = 18.85 A.[^18] 14.50 A is inside that. The 1.45 keeps small overloads from deteriorating the cable.[^19] A rewireable fuse to BS 3036 has a much higher I2: up to twice its rating, with the rating matched to the cable.[^22] So 2 × 10 = 20.00 A would pass the cable's 18.85 A. The cure is to keep the fuse's In to 0.725 Iz.[^23] That is Cf = 0.725.[^24] Now the cable needs Iz ≥ 10 ÷ 0.725 = 13.79 A. Then 1.45 × 13.79 = 20.00 A, which meets the fuse's I2 exactly. That works because 0.725 is 1.45 ÷ 2.

In the showroom, the motor's line current, 23.08 A, sets a 25 A breaker. But the six cables from the starter carry a winding's current. The starter's relay is set to that current, 13.33 A.[^37] For three-phase circuits, n singles count as n/3 circuits.[^42] So the six cables count as two circuits.[^43] Bunched together, they take Cg 0.80.[^25] Take Ca as 1.00 here, a practice value. Then they need It ≥ 16.66 A, which is 1.5 mm². **Size the cable for its hottest place: It ≥ In ÷ (the factors acting together).**[^12] **And size it for the current that finally operates its device: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.**[^18]

analogy.text: Think of a hoist whose overload cut-out lets the load run 45% past the plate rating before it stops it. The rope has to hold that 45% for as long as the cut-out takes. So you check the rope against the cut-out's point, not the plate. Now fit a cut-out that lets the load reach twice the plate rating. You either fit a heavier rope, or you lower the plate rating to 0.725 of what the rope is good for. A warm, crowded or lagged run is a rope that has lost some strength. You size for its weakest length.
analogy.breaks: A rope fails by force, at once. A cable fails by heat, over time. A small overload for a long time can do the damage a large one does quickly. That is why I2 comes with a time. It is also why the cable is allowed 1.45 Iz rather than Iz while the device decides.

practice.text:
- Start from Ib (lesson 1). Choose In: the smallest standard rating, or the setting, not below Ib.[^5] Choose the device type for the starting current.[^54] Type B trips instantly at 3 to 5 In.[^34] Type C trips at 5 to 10 In.[^35] Type D trips at 10 to 20 In.[^36] A motor or discharge lighting takes much more current starting than running.[^30] Its starting current may call for a higher In.[^55]
- Walk the route. For each part of it, list the factors acting there. Ca covers the ambient of that part. Cg applies where the cable is grouped, and it counts the circuit itself. Ci applies where the cable passes through insulation. Cf = 0.725 applies behind a BS 3036 rewireable fuse.[^24] You may leave a cable out of the group if it will carry not more than 30% of its grouped rating.[^14]
- For each part, work It ≥ In ÷ (the factors acting together). Design to the highest.[^2] Read the column of the reference method that cuts Iz the most.[^13]
- Pick the smallest CSA whose tabulated figure is at least It. Then Iz = that figure × the same factors, except Cf. Check Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.[^4]
- Check I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.[^8] Breakers to BS EN 60898 and fuses to BS 88 meet it once Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds.[^51] A BS 3036 fuse needs Cf. For a thermal relay in a motor circuit, read its own curve from the maker.[^52]

**Rule of thumb:** each factor is heat the table did not allow for, so it belongs to a place on the run. Multiply only the ones that share a place. The tables are in Appendix 4 of BS 7671.[^56] That appendix is informative.[^57] Its tables are the usual way to show the cable will not overheat.

**Worked example:** the showroom motor, with Ib 23.08 A, a star-delta starter and a 20 °C room. We choose a 25 A type C breaker, the type for small motors.[^35] The six singles from starter to motor carry a winding's current, 13.33 A. The starter's thermal relay is set to it.[^37] That setting is never higher than the phase current.[^38] The cables are sized on it too.[^40] Six singles are two three-phase circuits.[^43] Bunched in one conduit, they take Cg 0.80.[^25] Table 4B1 starts at 25 °C, where it gives 1.02.[^45] Take Ca as 1.00 here, a practice value. Then It ≥ 13.33 ÷ (1.00 × 0.80) = 16.66 A. In Table 4E1A, Reference Method B, 3 or 4 cables, 1 mm² carries 15 A, which is too little.[^49] 1.5 mm² carries 20 A.[^50] Iz = 20 × 1.00 × 0.80 = 16.00 A. So the relay must operate by 1.45 × 16.00 = 23.20 A. Read that from its maker's curve.[^52]

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying factors that never act together: 24.18 A where 21.28 A is right.[^2]
- Designing to the easier section or reference method.[^13]
- Leaving the circuit itself out of Cg.
- A rewireable fuse without Cf: its I2 passes the cable's 1.45 Iz.[^22]
- Sizing a star-delta motor's six cables on the line current. They carry a winding's current.[^41]
- Leaving an overload unchecked. It heats the conductors and, over time, damages insulation, joints and terminations.[^9] It can lead to fire.[^58]

b1.q: State a hazard of an overload current in a circuit, and explain how the design keeps a small overload from harming the cable.

points.text: An overload heats the circuit conductors well above the temperature they were chosen for.
points.cite: Professional Electrician (NICEIC), how the overload requirements of BS 7671 are applied, in research

points.text: Over time that heat damages the insulation, joints and terminations and what surrounds them. It can lead to fire.
points.cite: Professional Electrician (NICEIC); IET Wiring Matters, Mythbuster #11 (November 2024), in research

points.text: I2, the current that finally operates the device, must not exceed 1.45 Iz. Then a small overload does not deteriorate the cable before the device opens.
points.cite: Slides p.29 to 32; IET, changes to Appendix 4, in research

points.text: A rewireable BS 3036 fuse needs more current to operate: its fusing factor is above 1.45. So its rating is kept to 0.725 Iz, which is Cf = 0.725.

b1.model: An overload makes the circuit conductors run hotter than the temperature they were chosen for. Over time that damages the insulation, joints and terminations and what surrounds them. It can lead to fire. The design guards the cable first with Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. Then it adds I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz. The current that finally makes the device operate must not exceed 1.45 times the cable's current-carrying capacity. So a small overload that lasts until the device opens does not deteriorate the cable. A rewireable fuse to BS 3036 can need up to about twice its rating to operate. So its rating is kept to 0.725 Iz, which is Cf.

summary.title: Device and cable
summary.for: The device protects the cable. Choose the device from Ib, then the cable from the device, where the cable runs hottest: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. The cable must also take the current that finally operates the device: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz. Both come from Regulation 433.1.1.
summary.rule:
Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, and I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × Ci × Cf), only the factors that act together
Iz = tabulated figure × the same factors, except Cf
BS 3036 fuse: Cf = 0.725 (1.45 ÷ 2)

Work It for each part of the run. Design to the highest, on the reference method that cuts Iz most.
Cg counts the circuit itself. A cable at no more than 30% of its grouped rating may be left out (Table 4C1 note 9).
BS EN 60898 breakers and BS 88 fuses meet I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz once Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds (Regulation 433.1.201).
A motor's thermal relay: In is its setting. Check its own curve.

traps.text: Multiplying factors that never act together, or designing to the easier section or reference method. On the heater circuit, 24.18 A is wrong and 21.28 A is right.
Leaving the circuit being installed out of Cg.
A rewireable fuse without Cf: its I2 can pass the cable's 1.45 Iz.

traps.text: Sizing a star-delta motor's six cables on the line current: they carry a winding's current.

traps.text: Reading 90 °C ratings when the starter's or motor's terminals are designed for less. Rate the cables at the terminals' temperature: at 70 °C, 1.5 mm² carries only 15.5 A.
